recipe: When combining multiple JS Promises concurrently, use the native Promise.all_iterable / Promise.all_settled_iterable / Promise.race_iterable bindings on js_sys::Promise rather than Rust futures combinators, as they match JS semantics exactly and avoid the Rust executor polling each child on every wake.
trigger_condition: You need to run multiple JavaScript Promises concurrently and want JS-native concurrency semantics without Rust executor overhead.
evidence: When your inputs are already JS Promise<T> values, the native Promise.all / Promise.allSettled / Promise.race bindings on js_sys::Promise are the idiomatic choice — they match JS semantics exactly and avoid the Rust executor polling each child on every wake.

evidence: The canonical recipe collects the promise-producing iterator straight into a typed Array<Promise<T>> via [Array::from_iter_typed] and hands it to the combinator — no turbofish on the elements, no intermediate Vec.

recipe: For heterogeneous Promise.all over promises resolving to different types, collect them into a Rust tuple and pass to Promise::all_tuple, then destructure the result via .into_tuple() back into a native Rust tuple.
trigger_condition: You need to await multiple JS Promises that resolve to different types and want a type-safe combined result.
evidence: When the promises resolve to different types, collect them into a Rust tuple and pass to Promise::all_tuple. The result is a typed ArrayTuple<(T1, T2, ..., Tn)> you can destructure via .into_tuple() back into a native Rust tuple.
